objectives: Say what a nest is and what it is for.
Name the four reasons birds build nests.
Use the words nest, clutch, incubate and hatch.
Recognise six different kinds of nest.
Describe how a bird builds a nest, step by step.
Watch birds without disturbing their nests.

sections.body:
A nest is a home that a bird builds to hold its eggs and to raise its babies. It is not a house for the whole family. A nest is a nursery that lasts a few weeks, and then the birds move on.

A nest has to do four jobs at the same time. It has to **hold the eggs** safely, so they do not roll out or fall. It has to **keep the eggs warm**, because an egg that goes cold will never become a chick. It has to **hide the eggs** from animals that want to eat them. And it has to **hold the chicks** while they are too small to fly.

Most birds build their nests out of things that are easy to find. Twigs and dry grass are the most common. Some birds use mud. Some use soft feathers, or animal hair, or even their own breast feathers. A spider's silk is strong and stretchy, and some birds use that too. The bird carries each piece in its beak and arranges it with its own body.

The nest is shaped for the bird's body. A bird that sits on the eggs needs a nest that fits it, wide enough to hold one egg and tight enough to keep the heat in. A bird with long legs needs a nest on top of a branch, so its tail does not drag on the ground.

A nest also tells you a story about the bird. A hidden nest in a hole belongs to a shy bird. A huge messy nest on top of a tree belongs to a bird that defends it with noise. A nest with a roof over it belongs to a bird that likes to think about tomorrow.

By the end of this article you will know why birds build nests, the words scientists use for eggs and chicks, the different kinds of nest you can spot, and how to watch birds without upsetting them.
examples: The nest is a nursery, not a house.
The bird keeps the eggs warm with her own body.
This is a hanging nest, made by a weaving bird.
sections.heading: What is a nest?

sections.body:
**To keep the eggs warm.** A bird's body is a furnace. A hen's egg has to stay near 37 °C, or the chick inside stops growing. The mother bird sits on the eggs and warms them. When the chicks hatch, she keeps sitting on them, because they are still cold and still small.

**To keep the eggs safe.** A nest on the ground is a lunch for a cat. A nest in a bush is a snack for a snake. A nest in a hole in a tree is much harder to reach, and that is why woodpeckers and many ducks use holes.

**To keep the weather out.** Rain and wind make an egg cold. A roof of leaves or mud keeps the rain running off. A nest built in a sheltered place, under a branch or in a hole, stays dry inside.

**To hold the chicks.** Most young birds cannot fly and cannot walk. They sit in the nest and wait to be fed. The nest has to hold them, and it has to keep them from falling out.

Some birds do without a nest at all. An **ostrich** scrapes a shallow hole in the sand. A **penguin** keeps a single egg on its feet, under a flap of skin. And the male **bowerbird** builds something that is not a nest at all: a careful display of blue feathers and shiny things, built to persuade a female bird to mate with him.
examples: The mother bird keeps the eggs warm.
The nest in the hole is harder for a snake to reach.
The penguin keeps the egg under his skin.
sections.heading: Why birds build nests at all

sections.body:
A **cup nest** is the most common kind. A robin makes one from moss and grass, and lines the inside with fine dry grass. A **saucer nest** is flatter and built on the ground, and a lark makes one in a scrape in the earth.

A **cavity nest** is a hole, usually in the trunk of a tree. A woodpecker cuts a round hole with her beak and lines it with soft wood chips. Many birds will use the same hole for years.

A **mud nest** is built from mud. A swallow carries wet mud in her beak and shapes it into a small cup under the edge of a roof, and it hardens like plaster. A cliff swallow builds a whole wall of little mud rooms.

A **hanging nest** dangles from a branch, woven so tightly that it does not swing too much. A golden oriole makes one from plant fibre and hair, and hangs it out of sight at the top of a tree.

A **platform nest** is big and flat, and it sits on top of a branch or a cliff. An eagle builds one that weighs hundreds of kilograms, and the same nest is used again and again for years, with a new layer of sticks added each time.

A **floating nest** sits on the water. A coot makes one out of weeds and leaves, and pushes it to a sheltered corner when the wind gets up. And a **burrow nest** is dug into a sandy bank, and it can have a long tunnel leading to a safe room at the end.
examples: The robin has made a cup nest in the hedge.
The swallow is building a mud nest under the roof.
The eagle's platform nest is the same one she used last year.
sections.heading: Every nest is different

sections.body:
Here are four words that bird scientists use, and they are useful for anyone watching birds.

A **nest** is the structure the bird builds to hold its eggs and chicks. **Clutch** means all the eggs that one bird lays in one nest, and the number of eggs in a clutch varies a lot: a goldfinch may lay one egg, a blackbird lays five or six, and a duck may lay twelve.

To **incubate** the eggs means to keep them warm so that they can grow. The bird sits on them and turns them with her beak, so that one side does not get pressed all the time.

To **hatch** means to come out of the egg. A chick hatches by pushing with its feet and chipping the shell from the inside. A chick usually cannot see well for its first few days, and it cannot fly for several weeks.

Two more words are worth knowing. A **brood** is a group of chicks that hatch at the same time, and a **nestling** is a young bird that is still in the nest. When the nestling's feathers are ready, it becomes a **fledgling**, and then it can fly.
examples: That is a nest, and it holds four eggs.
The clutch of eggs is in the nest.
The chicks hatched yesterday, and they cannot fly yet.
sections.heading: The words about eggs and chicks

terms.example: The nest in the apple tree is full of twigs.
terms.gloss: The structure a bird builds to hold its eggs and raise its chicks.

terms.example: The blackbird's clutch has five eggs in it.
terms.gloss: All the eggs that one bird lays in one nest, counted together.

terms.example: The mother bird is incubating her eggs.
terms.gloss: To keep eggs warm so that the chicks inside can grow. The parent bird does it by sitting on them.

terms.example: One chick hatched this morning, and it is still wet.
terms.gloss: To come out of an egg. A chick hatches by pushing the shell from the inside.

sections.body:
Building a nest takes days of work, and the bird does it alone, piece by piece. Here is how it usually goes.

First, the bird **chooses the site**. She tries a few places and picks the one that is sheltered, hidden and near food. She may test the same branch for several days before she starts.

Second, she **collects the material**. Twigs come first, because a nest needs a frame. Then softer things come: grass, leaves, plant fibre, hair, feathers, and in some nests a little spider silk to hold it all together.

Third, she **shapes it**. The bird pushes and turns the material with her breast and her feet, weaving it round and round. This is the part that takes the longest.

Fourth, she **lines the inside**. The lining is soft and warm, and it keeps the eggs from touching the rough frame. Some birds add their own breast feathers, which they can pull out later and use as a blanket.

And last, she **finishes and checks**. She sits in the nest to see if it is the right size, and she repairs the edges every day after that, because a nest gets knocked about by wind and rain.
examples: The bird is carrying a twig to the nest.
She weaves the grass around the twigs.
The nest has a soft lining inside.
sections.heading: How a bird builds a nest
steps: The bird chooses a sheltered site near food.
She collects twigs first, then soft material.
She weaves the material round and round to shape the nest.
She lines the inside with something soft and warm.
She sits in the nest to check the size, and repairs it every day.

sections.body:
Watching a nest is one of the finest pleasures there is. But the nest is a busy home, and a nest that is disturbed can lose its eggs. So here is how to be a good guest.

**Stay low and keep quiet.** Sit down near the tree, not underneath it. A shadow over a nest can make the birds think a predator is there.

**Never climb to a nest.** In many countries it is against the law to take a nest or an egg, and in every country it can hurt the birds badly.

**Keep a good distance.** If the parent birds are coming and going calmly, you are far enough away. If they are calling and hovering and complaining, move back.

**Never touch the eggs or the chicks.** A baby bird that has been touched by a human can smell like a predator, and the parents may then abandon it.

**Leave the empty nest alone.** Many birds use the same nest year after year, and the shells and feathers inside are part of the nest now. Swallows come back to the very same mud nest every spring.

And if you find a chick on the ground, leave it. It is often not in trouble at all. It is learning to fly, and its parents are watching from the tree.
examples: I will sit down and keep quiet, and watch from here.
I will not climb up to look at the nest.
I will keep my distance, because the birds are nervous.
sections.heading: Watching birds without disturbing them

item.summary: Birds build nests for four good reasons, and every species has its own design. After reading this you can say what a nest is for, name the parts of an egg, recognise six kinds of nest, and watch birds without disturbing them.
item.title: Why Do Birds Build Nests?
